title: State v. Contreras-Sanchez
description: Whether geofence warrants, which allow law enforcement to obtain cell phone location data from tech companies, violate the Minnesota Constitution's protection against unreasonable searches, specifically regarding privacy expectations and the particularity requirement for warrants.
plaintiff_argument: Contreras-Sanchez argued that geofence warrants are unconstitutional general warrants, or at least this specific warrant lacked probable cause, was not sufficiently particular in its geographic scope and timeframe, and granted law enforcement unchecked discretion.
defendant_argument: The State argued that there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in location data stored by Google, thus no warrant is needed, or alternatively, the geofence warrant was supported by probable cause and was sufficiently particular.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' decision, ruling that the geofence warrant used to obtain location data violated the Minnesota Constitution's particularity requirement, but also held that geofence warrants are not categorically unconstitutional and that probable cause existed for this warrant.

title: Thigpen v. Best Home Care
description: Whether the penalty under Minnesota law for obtaining unemployment benefit overpayments through misrepresentation violates the Excessive Fines Clauses of the United States and Minnesota Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Christopher Thigpen, argued that the 40 percent penalty, 1 percent monthly interest, and 10-year bar on future unemployment benefits for misrepresentation constitute an unconstitutionally excessive punishment under the Excessive Fines Clauses.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED), argued that the statutory penalties for unemployment benefit misrepresentation are not unconstitutionally excessive and do not violate the Excessive Fines Clauses.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals, concluding that the punishment under Minnesota law for unemployment benefit misrepresentation overpayments is not grossly disproportional to the offense and therefore does not violate the Excessive Fines Clauses.

title: Jurgensen v. Dave Perkins Contracting, Inc.
description: Whether the statutory cap on attorney fees in workers' compensation cases, and the denial of excess fees, is constitutional and whether a recent amendment to the cap applies retroactively.
plaintiff_argument: Attorney Borken, representing the relator, argued that the 2024 amendment to the attorney fee cap should apply retroactively, that the WCCA erred by not automatically approving the unobjected-to excess fee, that the statutory fee cap violates the Contracts Clause of the Minnesota Constitution, and that the WCCA erred in denying excess fees under the Irwin factors.
defendant_argument: The employer-respondents took no position on the excess fees, but the Minnesota Attorney General intervened to defend the constitutionality of the statutory cap, arguing against retroactivity, for the WCCA's decision, and for the constitutionality of the cap.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the Workers' Compensation Court of Appeals, ruling that the 2024 amendment to the attorney fee cap does not apply retroactively, the WCCA did not err in denying excess fees, and the statutory fee cap does not violate the Contracts Clause.

title: Simon v. Demuth
description: Whether a legislative quorum requires a majority of the total number of seats in each house, or a majority of the total current legislators (excluding vacant seats).
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that a quorum requires a majority of the total number of possible seats in each house, as prescribed by law, not just the current number of seated legislators.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that a quorum requires a majority of the total number of current legislators, meaning vacant seats should not be counted.
decision_outcome: The court held that the quorum clause in the Minnesota Constitution requires a majority of the total number of seats of which each house may consist to constitute a quorum, meaning 68 members for the House of Representatives.

title: In re Benson
description: Whether a civilly committed person may waive their statutory right to counsel, with the plaintiff arguing they may and the defendant arguing they may not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Michael Benson, argued that the right to counsel established in Minnesota Statutes section 253D.20 is waivable, and he has a constitutional right to self-representation.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Commissioner of Human Services, argued that the right to counsel in civil commitment cases is not waivable, and civilly committed people must always be represented by an attorney.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' decision, concluding that the right to counsel in civil commitment cases is waivable, provided the waiver is knowing and intelligent, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: MacDonald v. Simon
description: Whether a person whose law license is suspended is "learned in the law" as required by the Minnesota Constitution for judicial office, and thus eligible to appear on the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: Michelle MacDonald argued that being "learned in the law" does not require an active law license and that the statutory requirement for a current license is unconstitutional.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of State argued that a suspended law license means MacDonald is not "learned in the law" and is therefore ineligible for judicial office and the ballot.
decision_outcome: The court denied Michelle MacDonald's petition, ruling that her suspended law license means she is not "learned in the law" and thus not constitutionally qualified to be a judge of the supreme court.

title: Jacobs v. City of Columbia Heights
description: Whether a petition to recall a city council member lawfully triggers a special recall election under Minnesota Statutes section 410.20 (2022) if it fails to allege malfeasance or nonfeasance, the constitutional prerequisites for recalling an elected municipal official.
plaintiff_argument: Jacobs argued that the recall petition failed to allege malfeasance or nonfeasance, the constitutional prerequisites for recalling an elected municipal official, and thus unlawfully triggered a special recall election.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the grounds for recall stated in the petition met the legal definition of malfeasance, thereby lawfully triggering the special recall election.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's decision, concluding that the recall petition did not meet the legal definitions of malfeasance or nonfeasance, and cancelled the special recall election.

title: Doe v. Minnesota
description: Whether the petition for further review filed by Mothers Offering Maternal Support should be granted.
plaintiff_argument: Mothers Offering Maternal Support argued that their petition for further review should be granted.
defendant_argument: Dr. Jane Doe, et al., and Governor of Minnesota, et al., argued that the petition for further review should be denied.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition of Mothers Offering Maternal Support for further review.

title: Schools Over Stadiums v. Thompson
description: Whether the Stadium Referendum, which seeks to disapprove select portions of Senate Bill No. 1, is valid under the Nevada Constitution's full-text requirement and statutory requirements for description of effect.
plaintiff_argument: The Stadium Referendum complies with the Nevada Constitution's full-text requirement and provides an adequate description of its effect, allowing voters to decide on state funding for the stadium project.
defendant_argument: The Stadium Referendum is invalid because it violates the full-text requirement of the Nevada Constitution and contains a legally inadequate and misleading description of its effect.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's judgment, declaring the Stadium Referendum invalid and enjoining its circulation and placement on the ballot.

title: Snell v. Walz
description: Whether the Emergency Management Act authorizes the Governor to declare a peacetime emergency for a pandemic and whether the Act constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The Emergency Management Act does not allow the Governor to declare a peacetime emergency in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Act is unconstitutional under the nondelegation doctrine because it delegates unrestrained lawmaking authority to the Governor.
defendant_argument: The Emergency Management Act authorizes the Governor to declare a peacetime emergency in response to a pandemic, and the Act provides for a constitutional delegation of legislative authority.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals, concluding that Governor Walz was authorized to declare a peacetime emergency in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and that the Emergency Management Act is not an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.

title: Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Hunt
description: Whether taxpayers and their association have standing to challenge the Re-Enfranchisement Act, which restores voting rights to felons, based on alleged unlawful disbursements of public funds for its implementation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Re-Enfranchisement Act violates the Minnesota Constitution by restoring only a single civil right (the right to vote) instead of multiple civil rights to felons, and that the use of public funds for voter education related to this allegedly unconstitutional act is unlawful, thereby conferring taxpayer and associational standing.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing because their challenge was to the substantive law itself, not a specific unlawful disbursement of public funds, and the expenditures for implementing the law were merely incidental.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, concluding that the Taxpayers and their Association lacked standing to challenge the Re-Enfranchisement Act.

title: Alliance Housing Incorporated v. County of Hennepin
description: Whether an institution of purely public charity uses its property in furtherance of its charitable purpose when it leases property to low-income individuals for personal residence.
plaintiff_argument: Alliance Housing argues that leasing its properties to low-income individuals for personal residence constitutes using the property in furtherance of its charitable purpose, thus qualifying for tax exemption.
defendant_argument: Hennepin County argues that Alliance Housing does not "use" its properties for an exempt purpose when it leases them to "non-exempt third parties" for personal residence, implying a "residence plus" factor is needed for tax exemption.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the tax court's decision, ruling that Alliance Housing's properties are exempt from property taxes.

title: Minnesota v. Malecha
description: Whether the good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule under the Minnesota Constitution applies to evidence obtained during a search incident to an arrest based on a quashed warrant that appeared active due to a clerical court error.
plaintiff_argument: The exclusionary rule should apply because the arrest warrant was quashed, making the search unlawful, and the good-faith exception should not extend to clerical errors by court administration under the Minnesota Constitution.
defendant_argument: The good-faith exception should apply because law enforcement reasonably relied on an apparently active warrant due to a clerical error by court administration, and excluding the evidence would not deter police misconduct.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the decision of the court of appeals and reinstated the district court's order dismissing the charges against Malecha.

title: Cruz-Guzman v. State
description: Whether racial imbalances in Minneapolis and Saint Paul public schools, as compared to other schools in the same school district, are sufficient, standing alone, to establish a violation of the Education Clause of the Minnesota Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The parents argued that racial imbalances in public schools automatically mean the Legislature has violated its duty to provide an adequate education, establishing a per se violation of the Education Clause without needing to prove state intent or causation.
defendant_argument: The State argued that racial imbalances alone do not violate the Education Clause without evidence of intentional racial segregation or that the imbalances caused an inadequate education, and that liability should be limited to issues over which the Legislature has control.
decision_outcome: The court held that racial imbalances in Minneapolis and Saint Paul public schools, standing alone, are not sufficient to establish a violation of the Education Clause, and that plaintiffs must prove these imbalances are a substantial factor in causing an inadequate education.

title: State v. Bell
description: Whether the exclusion of the public from a courtroom during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to a public trial, with the plaintiff arguing it did and the defendant arguing it did not or was justified.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Abraham Isaac Bell, argued that the complete exclusion of all spectators, including his family, from the courtroom, even with a video feed to an adjacent room, violated his Sixth Amendment right to a public trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Minnesota, argued that the courtroom restrictions implemented due to the COVID-19 pandemic were too trivial to constitute a closure implicating the Sixth Amendment, or if a closure occurred, it was constitutionally justifiable due to public health concerns.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' decision and remanded the case to the district court for additional factual findings on whether reasonable alternatives to courtroom closure were considered and if the closure was broader than necessary.

title: Kranz v. City of Bloomington
description: Whether an unconstitutional provision in a proposed city-charter amendment can be severed, allowing the remaining valid language to be placed on the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The unconstitutional section 4.08 should be severed, and the remaining valid sections of the proposed charter amendment should be submitted to the voters.
defendant_argument: Section 4.08 is integral to the proposed charter amendment's purpose and cannot be severed, thus the entire amendment should be rejected from the ballot.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, concluding that the unconstitutional section 4.08 was not severable from the rest of the proposed charter amendment.

title: Schroeder v. Simon
description: Whether the Minnesota Constitution requires automatic restoration of voting rights for felons upon release from incarceration, and whether the current statute (Minn. Stat. § 609.165) violates the fundamental right to vote or equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Minnesota Constitution mandates automatic restoration of voting rights for felons upon release from incarceration, and that Minn. Stat. § 609.165 violates their fundamental right to vote and the equal protection principle due to its disproportionate racial impact.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Minnesota Constitution requires an affirmative act of government to restore voting rights, not automatic restoration upon release, and that Minn. Stat. § 609.165 is constitutional, neither violating the fundamental right to vote nor equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that the Minnesota Constitution does not require automatic restoration of voting rights for felons upon release from incarceration, and that Minn. Stat. § 609.165 does not violate the fundamental right to vote or the equal protection principle.

title: Under the Rainbow Early Education Center v. County of Goodhue
description: Whether an early childhood education center qualifies as a "seminary of learning" for property tax exemption under state law, specifically Minn. Const., art. X, § 1, and Minn. Stat. § 272.02, subd. 5.
plaintiff_argument: Rainbow argued that it is an educational institution providing a general curriculum in a thorough and comprehensive manner, meeting the criteria for a tax-exempt seminary of learning based on its licensure, programming, and Parent Aware rating.
defendant_argument: Goodhue County argued that Rainbow's evidence was insufficient to prove it reduced the burden on public education or that its programming could be readily assimilated into the public school system, and suggested Rainbow was merely a daycare provider.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the tax court's decision, ruling that Rainbow was entitled to summary judgment and qualified for the property tax exemption as a seminary of learning.

title: State v. Hassan
description: Whether a mandatory sentence of life without the possibility of release imposed on a 21-year-old defendant is unconstitutionally cruel under Article I, Section 5, of the Minnesota Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Hassan argues that the State presented insufficient evidence to support his conviction and that a mandatory sentence of life without the possibility of release imposed on a 21-year-old defendant is unconstitutionally cruel under Article I, Section 5, of the Minnesota Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State argues that there was sufficient evidence to support the conviction and that the mandatory sentence of life without the possibility of release is not unconstitutionally cruel.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, upholding Omar Nur Hassan's conviction for first-degree premeditated murder and his mandatory sentence of life without the possibility of release.

title: Shefa v.  Ellison
description: Whether the Minnesota Legislature violated the state's constitution by requiring a unanimous vote from the Board of Pardons to grant a pardon.
plaintiff_argument: The unanimity requirement is unconstitutional because it impermissibly thwarts the governor's independent pardon power and violates the separation of powers by allowing the chief justice to unilaterally veto an executive function.
defendant_argument: The unanimity requirement is constitutional because the pardon power is vested in the Board of Pardons, not solely the governor, and the chief justice's participation is explicitly provided for in the constitution, thus not violating separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's finding that the unanimity requirement violates the pardon provision and affirmed the district court's finding that it does not violate the separation-of-powers provision, concluding that the unanimity requirement for pardons is constitutional.

title: State v. Sargent
description: Whether law enforcement officers may expand the scope of a traffic stop to investigate a passenger's potential violation of a pretrial release condition when such a violation is not considered criminal activity.
plaintiff_argument: The officer's questioning about pretrial release conditions improperly expanded the traffic stop, violating constitutional rights against unreasonable searches and seizures because a pretrial release violation is not a crime.
defendant_argument: An officer may expand a traffic stop to investigate a potential pretrial release violation if the actions are reasonable under Terry, even if the violation is not a crime.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's decision, vacated Sargent's conviction for illegal possession of ammunition, and granted his motion to suppress evidence, ruling that the expansion of the traffic stop was an unlawful seizure.

title: State v. Mikell
description: Whether the State violated Mikell's rights under the Minnesota Uniform Mandatory Disposition of Detainers Act (UMDDA) or his constitutional right to a speedy trial by dismissing and later refiling charges more than 6 months after his request for final disposition.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the UMDDA only applies to pending complaints, and once charges are dismissed, the right to disposition ceases. They also contended that the period between dismissal and refiling should not count towards speedy trial delay if done in good faith.
defendant_argument: Mikell argued that his DANCO convictions violated the UMDDA because the State failed to bring him to trial within 6 months of his request, and the district court lacked jurisdiction. He also claimed his constitutional right to a speedy trial was violated due to the delay, and the district court abused its discretion by not dismissing the complaint.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the court of appeals, concluding that the State did not violate Mikell's rights under the UMDDA or his constitutional right to a speedy trial, and the district court did not abuse its discretion by declining to dismiss the complaint.
